summary: This opinion-style piece argues that severe weather is causing a growing number of transit delays and cancellations worldwide, citing events from September and October 2023 in the US, Germany, Indonesia, Vietnam and elsewhere. It describes human and economic costs, including a $60 billion annual global estimate, and calls for resilient infrastructure, better forecasting and technology, and international cooperation.
one_line: A call for weather-resilient transit infrastructure and global cooperation, citing 2023 storm-related delays and cancellations and their human and economic costs.
key_facts: On October 3, 2023, a powerful nor'easter struck the northeastern corridor of the United States, causing over 500 flight cancellations and delays at all major airports in the region.
On September 19, 2023, a tropical storm disrupted the metro system in Atlanta, stranding thousands of commuters.
On October 21, 2023, a hailstorm in Munich, Germany, damaged rail tracks and signaling equipment, halting services and stranding passengers for hours.
Boston commuter Linda Rodriguez said she was stranded at South Station for over six hours on October 3rd: "Nothing was moving."
Excessive heat can warp rail tracks, while cold snaps can cause frozen switches and broken lines.
A flash flood in Jakarta, Indonesia, reported on September 27, 2023, submerged roads and halted the city's public bus system, cutting off thousands of workers.
A Global Economic Policy Initiative study released September 30, 2023 estimated weather-related transit delays and cancellations cost the global economy around $60 billion annually.
A typhoon in Vietnam on October 15, 2023 disrupted textile exports, illustrating how local floods can disrupt global supply chains.
The Netherlands has raised highways to prevent flooding and designed water-absorbent urban landscapes.
On September 22, 2023, Tokyo authorities used early warning systems to anticipate severe wind and shut down the train system before the storm hit.
Lower-income communities that rely more on public transportation are disproportionately affected by transit outages.
The piece recommends smart infrastructure, predictive maintenance, flexible work policies, and global cooperation on adaptation.
